steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on improving how reinforcement learning models for social robot navigation are trained and evaluated so that they generalize better. Motivate the problem with current training practices and state what the study does.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Robots entering human spaces; social norms are hard to codify
- Approaches to social navigation; interactive RL with Social Force / ORCA pedestrians
- How Social Force and ORCA work; homogeneous training data
- Criticism of single-model training
- This work: three RL models, better training and evaluation

  - ORCA: prunes action space (permissible future velocities) each time step -> guaranteed collision avoidance

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Autonomous mobile robots are moving more and more into human spaces. For this to go on smoothly and successfully, a number of social and technological factors have to be considered carefully. Social norms can be different depending on the context and the culture, and they are often hard to codify. For example, ideas of personal space may be different for pedestrian traffic on the sidewalk compared to an open space, for indoors compared to outdoors, for the speed of walking traffic, or for the time of day, and so on.

Many approaches have been proposed for making mobile robots that navigate in socially appropriate ways. There is work that tries to explicitly codify human preferences when navigating around a robot, but this is still a nascent field of research, and most social navigation approaches try to emulate human behavior instead. One modern trend is to learn to copy human-like behavior through interactive RL training, meaning that the pedestrian agents can react to the robot agent, instead of using prerecorded data. This is usually done in an environment where the pedestrian agents follow predefined deterministic social navigation algorithms, most commonly either Social Force or ORCA.

Social Force explicitly models hypothetical pairwise attraction and repulsion forces between agents and obstacles. In ORCA, every agent prunes its action space, which is the set of permissible future velocities, at every time step, and this gives a mathematical guarantee that collisions are avoided. Both of these models have built-in assumptions that make the training data homogeneous.

Even in some of the most prominent RL social navigation research, the navigation models are trained in one environment with fixed specifications, and on pedestrian navigation data that is generated by only one behavioral model.

- Criticism of single-model training
  - training on one pedestrian model criticized in the field
  - proof-of-concept: agent goes straight to goal, stops if pedestrian too close -> beats ORCA-based agents on time to goal
  - authors: ORCA-only training/testing not a good indicator of real-world performance
  - need to examine homogeneous pedestrian modeling and simple training/evaluation; challenge status quo
- This work
  - improve CADRL, LSTM-RL, SARL through training (quantitative and qualitative)
  - previous results limited by simple test environments -> more meaningful generalizability evaluation
  - mixed Social Force / ORCA pedestrians; curriculum of environment types; harder unseen test environments (crowd density, environment size)
  - code at github.com/RAISE-Lab/soc-nav-training

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Autonomous mobile robots are moving more and more into human spaces. For this to go on smoothly and successfully, a number of social and technological factors have to be considered carefully. Social norms can be different depending on the context and the culture, and they are often hard to codify. For example, ideas of personal space may be different for pedestrian traffic on the sidewalk compared to an open space, for indoors compared to outdoors, for the speed of walking traffic, or for the time of day, and so on.

Many approaches have been proposed for making mobile robots that navigate in socially appropriate ways. There is work that tries to explicitly codify human preferences when navigating around a robot, but this is still a nascent field of research, and most social navigation approaches try to emulate human behavior instead. One modern trend is to learn to copy human-like behavior through interactive RL training, meaning that the pedestrian agents can react to the robot agent, instead of using prerecorded data. This is usually done in an environment where the pedestrian agents follow predefined deterministic social navigation algorithms, most commonly either Social Force or ORCA.

Social Force explicitly models hypothetical pairwise attraction and repulsion forces between agents and obstacles. In ORCA, every agent prunes its action space, which is the set of permissible future velocities, at every time step, and this gives a mathematical guarantee that collisions are avoided. Both of these models have built-in assumptions that make the training data homogeneous.

Even in some of the most prominent RL social navigation research, the navigation models are trained in one environment with fixed specifications, and on pedestrian navigation data that is generated by only one behavioral model.

Training on data that is generated only by one model of pedestrian behavior has been criticized in the field. A proof-of-concept experiment in that work shows the limitations of relying on one deterministic model. The authors showed that a policy where an agent goes straight to its goal and stops whenever a pedestrian gets too close does better than ORCA-based agents in the time it takes to reach the goal. They argue that this means that training and testing only on pedestrian data generated by ORCA, which many current works do, is not a good indicator of how the robot will perform in the real world. So, to make better social navigation behaviors for mobile robots possible, it is important that we scientifically examine how well the current practices work, namely modeling pedestrians homogeneously and keeping training and evaluation methods simple, and challenge the status quo.

In this work we look at how training can improve the quantitative and qualitative performance of three state-of-the-art RL social navigation models (CADRL, LSTM-RL, and SARL). We also show that the results in previous works are limited because their testing environments are simple. In response, we present approaches for evaluating their generalizability in a more meaningful way. For this, in this study we:

- Do interactive RL training in an environment where some pedestrians are modeled by Social Force and some are modeled by ORCA.

- Use a curriculum of different environment types during training.

- Do performance evaluation in unseen testing environments that are harder than the ones used in training, by increasing both the crowd density and the environment size.

The code we used for these experiments is publicly available at: github.com/RAISE-Lab/soc-nav-training.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Autonomous mobile robots are increasingly expanding into human spaces. For this process to continue smoothly and successfully, a number of social and technological factors must be carefully considered. Social norms can vary depending on context and culture, and are often difficult to codify. For example, conceptions of personal space may differ for pedestrian traffic on the sidewalk versus an open space, indoors versus outdoors, with the speed of walking traffic, or with the time of day, among others.

A myriad of approaches have been proposed for creating mobile robots that navigate in socially appropriate ways. While some work aims to explicitly codify human preferences when navigating around a robot [1], this remains a nascent field of research, and most social navigation approaches instead seek to emulate human behavior. One modern trend is learning to replicate human-like behavior through interactive RL training (i.e. where pedestrian agents can react to the robot agent, rather than using prerecorded data). This is usually done in an environment where pedestrian agents follow predefined deterministic social navigation algorithms, most commonly either Social Force [2] or ORCA [3].

Social Force explicitly models hypothetical pairwise attraction and repulsion forces between agents and obstacles. In ORCA, each agent prunes its action space (permissible future velocities) at every time step, which allows a mathematical guarantee of collision avoidance. Both of these models carry intrinsic assumptions that lead to homogeneous training data.

Even in some of the most prominent RL social navigation research, navigation models are trained in a single environment with fixed specifications and on pedestrian navigation data generated by only one behavioral model [4,5,6].

Training on data generated exclusively by a single model of pedestrian behavior has been criticized in the field [7]. A proof-of-concept experiment in that work illustrates the limitations of relying on a single deterministic model: the authors showed that a policy in which an agent goes straight towards its goal and stops whenever a pedestrian gets too close outperforms ORCA-based agents in time elapsed to reach the goal [7]. They argue that training and testing exclusively on pedestrian data generated by ORCA, as many contemporary works do, is therefore not a good indicator of real-world performance. Hence, to enable better social navigation behaviors for mobile robots, it is crucial to scientifically examine the efficacy of current practices – homogeneous modeling of pedestrians and simple training and evaluation methods – and to challenge the status quo.

In this work, we explore how training can improve the quantitative and qualitative performance of three state-of-the-art RL social navigation models (CADRL [5], LSTM-RL [6], and SARL [4]). We also show that the results presented in previous works are limited by the simplicity of their testing environments, and in response we present approaches for evaluating their generalizability more meaningfully. To this end, in this study we:

- Conduct interactive RL training in an environment where some pedestrians are modeled by Social Force and some by ORCA.

- Use a curriculum of different environment types during training.

- Evaluate performance in unseen testing environments that are more challenging than those used in training, by increasing both crowd density and environment size.

The code used for these experiments is publicly available at: github.com/RAISE-Lab/soc-nav-training.

References:
[1] Christoforos Mavrogiannis, Patrícia Alves-Oliveira, Wil Thomason, and Ross A. Knepper. Social momentum: Design and evaluation of a framework for socially competent robot navigation. J. Hum.-Robot Interact. , 11(2), feb 2022.
[2] Dirk Helbing and Péter Molnár. Social force model for pedestrian dynamics. Physical Review E , 51(5):4282–4286, May 1995.
[3] Jur Van Den Berg, Stephen J Guy, Ming Lin, and Dinesh Manocha. Reciprocal n-body collision avoidance. In Robotics research , pages 3–19. Springer, 2011.
[4] Changan Chen, Yuejiang Liu, Sven Kreiss, and Alexandre Alahi. Crowd-robot interaction: Crowd-aware robot navigation with attention-based deep reinforcement learning. In 2019 International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) , pages 6015–6022. IEEE, 2019.
[5] Yu Fan Chen, Miao Liu, Michael Everett, and Jonathan P How. Decentralized non-communicating multiagent collision avoidance with deep reinforcement learning. In 2017 IEEE international conference on robotics and automation (ICRA) , pages 285–292. IEEE, 2017.
[6] Michael Everett, Yu Fan Chen, and Jonathan P How. Motion planning among dynamic, decision-making agents with deep reinforcement learning. In 2018 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) , pages 3052–3059. IEEE, 2018.
[7] Christoforos I. Mavrogiannis, Francesca Baldini, Allan Wang, Dapeng Zhao, Pete Trautman, Aaron Steinfeld, and Jean Oh. Core challenges of social robot navigation: A survey. CoRR , abs/2103.05668, 2021.
